cards.a: Every device connects point-to-point to a central device (a hub or, in practice, a switch). It is the physical foundation of modern Ethernet wiring: each host has its own UTP link, and logical behavior depends on whether the center is a hub (shared) or a switch (microsegmented).

cards.q: What collision-domain and behavior differences arise from a hub, switch, or router at the center of a star?
cards.a: A hub (L1) creates one collision domain for all nodes and repeats frames to every port in half-duplex CSMA/CD. A switch (L2) gives one collision domain per port via microsegmentation with full-duplex and MAC learning. A router (L3) isolates per interface and forms a subnet boundary with different L3 networks per interface.

cards.q: What are the advantages of a star topology?
cards.a: Fault isolation — a bad cable/port affects only that link while the rest keep working; easy adds/moves by plugging a device into a spare port; scalability by adding ports/switches; and, with a switch, full duplex, per-host bandwidth, and security segmentation via VLANs.

cards.q: What is the main disadvantage of a star topology and how is it mitigated?
cards.a: The central device is a single point of failure. Mitigation uses redundant switches plus dual-homed hosts/server NICs and HSRP/VRRP gateways.

cards.q: Where do star topologies appear in enterprise design?
cards.a: At the access layer, every endpoint star-wires to its access switch. In spine-leaf, each leaf connects to each spine, forming a logical star/mesh hybrid. In a collapsed core, two distribution switches form a redundant star for each access block.

cards.q: What commands configure a star access port and add gateway redundancy?
cards.a: Use 'interface GigabitEthernet0/1' with 'switchport access vlan 10' and 'spanning-tree portfast' for the host port (no STP delay), and on Vlan10 configure HSRP with 'standby 10 ip 10.1.10.1' for gateway redundancy.

cards.q: True or misleading: a star with a hub center is fully full-duplex. What is the truth?
cards.a: Misleading. A star with a hub center is physical star but logical bus — all nodes share the same collision domain. Full duplex depends on the center being a switch.

cards.q: How does a star differ from a bus when a single cable fails?
cards.a: In a star, a break in one cable isolates only that host — the rest keep working. A bus, by contrast, fails on a single cable break.

cards.q: What is the single point of failure in a star and what is the fix?
cards.a: The center switch is the SPOF. The fix is a redundant switch pair plus dual-homed hosts, with HSRP/VRRP for the gateway.

cards.q: In the star Quick Review, how do hub, switch, and router centers compare for L2 effect and collision domains?
cards.a: A hub repeats and shares, giving 1 collision domain for all. A switch does MAC learning with separate domains per port, giving N (one per port). A router provides L3 subnets with collision domains isolated per interface. Central fault impact affects only the bad link, and the SPOF (the center) is mitigated by redundancy plus HSRP.
